author: A. Tversky & D. Kahneman
title: Availability heuristic
statement: People judge frequency or likelihood by how easily examples come to mind.
rationale: Vivid testimonials and recent events skew risk perception; present base rates alongside stories.
audit_check: Are risk and frequency claims supported by numbers, not only vivid anecdotes?
license: Original summary written for this knowledge base (free to use); cite the original source

author: D. Kahneman & A. Tversky
title: Representativeness heuristic
statement: People judge probability by similarity to a prototype, neglecting base rates.
rationale: Users judge legitimacy by resemblance to familiar brands; consistent, conventional design signals legitimacy (and phishing exploits this).
audit_check: Does the product look consistent with its own brand across all touchpoints so users can spot impostors?
license: Original summary written for this knowledge base (free to use); cite the original source

author: P. C. Wason
title: Confirmation bias
statement: Tendency to search for, interpret and remember information that confirms prior beliefs.
rationale: Researchers and stakeholders over-weight findings that confirm their designs; use structured analysis and disconfirming questions.
audit_check: Were findings analyzed against pre-set criteria, including evidence against the team’s hypothesis?
license: Original summary written for this knowledge base (free to use); cite the original source

author: W. Samuelson & R. Zeckhauser
title: Status quo bias
statement: Preference for the current state of affairs; changes are perceived as losses.
rationale: Users resist redesigns and stick with defaults; migrate gradually and explain benefits.
audit_check: Do redesigns preserve familiar paths or explain changes?
license: Original summary written for this knowledge base (free to use); cite the original source

author: H. Arkes & C. Blumer
title: Sunk cost fallacy
statement: Continuing an endeavor because of previously invested resources rather than future value.
rationale: Long forms and onboarding create commitment; exploiting it to retain users (e.g., hard-to-cancel after long setup) is manipulative.
audit_check: Are cancel and exit options equally easy regardless of how much the user has invested?
license: Original summary written for this knowledge base (free to use); cite the original source

author: R. Thaler
title: Endowment effect
statement: People value things more once they own them.
rationale: Free trials and customization create ownership feelings; be transparent about what happens at trial end.
audit_check: Is trial-to-paid conversion transparent with advance reminders?
license: Original summary written for this knowledge base (free to use); cite the original source

author: Classic social psychology (Asch 1951; Cialdini 1984)
title: Bandwagon effect / social proof
statement: People adopt beliefs or behaviors because many others do.
rationale: Ratings, reviews and usage counts influence decisions; they must be genuine and current.
audit_check: Are social proof claims (counts, reviews, "X people viewing") genuine and verifiable?
license: Original summary written for this knowledge base (free to use); cite the original source

author: S. Milgram
title: Authority bias
statement: Tendency to attribute greater accuracy to the opinion of an authority figure.
rationale: Expert endorsements and certifications raise trust; fake badges are deceptive.
audit_check: Are trust badges, certifications and endorsements real and linked to verification?
license: Original summary written for this knowledge base (free to use); cite the original source

source_org: S. Worchel, J. Lee & A. Adewole
author: S. Worchel, J. Lee & A. Adewole
title: Scarcity effect
statement: Items perceived as scarce are perceived as more valuable.
rationale: Low-stock and limited-time messages drive urgency; fake scarcity is a deceptive pattern and illegal in many jurisdictions.
audit_check: Are scarcity and urgency messages accurate and based on real inventory/time limits?
citation: S. Worchel, J. Lee & A. Adewole (1975).
license: Original summary written for this knowledge base (free to use); cite the original source

author: A. Gouldner; R. Cialdini
title: Reciprocity
statement: People feel obliged to return favors.
rationale: Giving value first (free tools, content) before asking for signup builds goodwill.
audit_check: Does the product give value before asking for personal information or payment?
license: Original summary written for this knowledge base (free to use); cite the original source

author: J. Freedman & S. Fraser (foot-in-the-door)
title: Commitment and consistency
statement: After a small commitment, people are more likely to agree to larger related requests.
rationale: Progressive engagement (small first step) increases completion; escalating commitments must stay honest.
audit_check: Do flows start with low-commitment steps and avoid bait-and-switch escalation?
license: Original summary written for this knowledge base (free to use); cite the original source

author: J. Freedman & S. Fraser
title: Foot-in-the-door technique
statement: Agreeing to a small request increases likelihood of agreeing to a larger one.
rationale: Start with easy micro-commitments (e.g., one question) in onboarding.
audit_check: Is the first step of signup/onboarding small and easy?
license: Original summary written for this knowledge base (free to use); cite the original source

author: R. Cialdini et al.
title: Door-in-the-face technique
statement: A large request refused first makes a subsequent smaller request more likely to be accepted.
rationale: Retention offers after a cancel request use this; acceptable if the user can still cancel easily.
audit_check: After a cancel request, can users still complete cancellation in one clear step?
license: Original summary written for this knowledge base (free to use); cite the original source

author: D. Kahneman & A. Tversky
title: Loss aversion
statement: Losses are felt about twice as strongly as equivalent gains.
rationale: Loss-framed messages motivate (e.g., "don’t lose your progress"), but shaming and threats are manipulative.
audit_check: Are loss-framed messages factual and free of guilt or shaming?
license: Original summary written for this knowledge base (free to use); cite the original source

author: A. Tversky & D. Kahneman
title: Framing effect
statement: Decisions change based on how equivalent information is presented.
rationale: Consent and pricing language must be neutral and clear.
audit_check: Are consequential options framed neutrally?
license: Original summary written for this knowledge base (free to use); cite the original source

author: A. Tversky & D. Kahneman
title: Anchoring bias
statement: Over-reliance on the first piece of information.
rationale: First price shown anchors value; genuine reference prices only.
audit_check: Are reference/strikethrough prices genuine?
license: Original summary written for this knowledge base (free to use); cite the original source

source_org: J. Huber, J. Payne & C. Puto
author: J. Huber, J. Payne & C. Puto
title: Decoy effect
statement: An inferior option changes preference between two others.
rationale: Pricing tables often use decoys; ensure each tier serves real needs.
audit_check: Does each pricing tier serve a real segment?
citation: J. Huber, J. Payne & C. Puto (1982).
license: Original summary written for this knowledge base (free to use); cite the original source

author: E. Johnson & D. Goldstein
title: Default bias
statement: People tend to accept pre-set options.
rationale: Defaults must favor users; never pre-check consent or paid add-ons.
audit_check: Are any consent, marketing or paid options pre-selected?
license: Original summary written for this knowledge base (free to use); cite the original source

source_org: S. Iyengar & M. Lepper; B. Schwartz
author: S. Iyengar & M. Lepper; B. Schwartz
title: Choice overload / paradox of choice
statement: Too many options can cause decision paralysis and lower satisfaction.
rationale: Curate, recommend and filter.
audit_check: Are option sets manageable or supported by filters and recommendations?
citation: S. Iyengar & M. Lepper; B. Schwartz (2000/2004).
license: Original summary written for this knowledge base (free to use); cite the original source

author: G. Ainslie; D. Laibson
title: Hyperbolic discounting / present bias
statement: People prefer smaller immediate rewards over larger later rewards.
rationale: Immediate value in onboarding matters; "buy now, pay later" exploits present bias.
audit_check: Is the immediate cost of deferred payment options made clear?
license: Original summary written for this knowledge base (free to use); cite the original source

author: D. Kahneman & A. Tversky
title: Planning fallacy
statement: People underestimate the time needed to complete tasks.
rationale: Show realistic time estimates for forms and setup ("about 10 minutes").
audit_check: Do long tasks show realistic time estimates?
license: Original summary written for this knowledge base (free to use); cite the original source

author: N. Weinstein
title: Optimism bias
statement: People believe they are less likely than others to experience negative events.
rationale: Users skip backups, security settings and insurance; make protective defaults automatic.
audit_check: Are protective behaviors (backups, 2FA, autosave) on by default?
license: Original summary written for this knowledge base (free to use); cite the original source

source_org: S. Lichtenstein, B. Fischhoff & L. Phillips
author: S. Lichtenstein, B. Fischhoff & L. Phillips
title: Overconfidence effect
statement: Subjective confidence exceeds objective accuracy.
rationale: Users skip review steps; show summaries before irreversible submission.
audit_check: Is there a review step before irreversible submissions?
citation: S. Lichtenstein, B. Fischhoff & L. Phillips (1982).
license: Original summary written for this knowledge base (free to use); cite the original source

author: J. Kruger & D. Dunning
title: Dunning–Kruger effect
statement: People with low ability in a domain overestimate their competence.
rationale: Self-rated skill in onboarding questionnaires is unreliable; infer from behavior.
audit_check: Does personalization rely on behavior rather than self-rated expertise alone?
license: Original summary written for this knowledge base (free to use); cite the original source

source_org: C. Camerer, G. Loewenstein & M. Weber
author: C. Camerer, G. Loewenstein & M. Weber
title: Curse of knowledge
statement: Experts find it hard to imagine not knowing what they know.
rationale: Teams write jargon and skip steps obvious to them; test copy with real users.
audit_check: Has copy been tested with people outside the team?
citation: C. Camerer, G. Loewenstein & M. Weber (1989).
license: Original summary written for this knowledge base (free to use); cite the original source

source_org: L. Ross, D. Greene & P. House
author: L. Ross, D. Greene & P. House
title: False consensus effect
statement: People overestimate how much others share their beliefs and behaviors.
rationale: Designers assume users behave like them; research with real users.
audit_check: Are design decisions based on research with actual users rather than team preference?
citation: L. Ross, D. Greene & P. House (1977).
license: Original summary written for this knowledge base (free to use); cite the original source

source_org: M. Norton, D. Mochon & D. Ariely
author: M. Norton, D. Mochon & D. Ariely
title: IKEA effect
statement: Higher value placed on self-assembled things.
rationale: Customization increases attachment.
audit_check: Is user-created content portable?
citation: M. Norton, D. Mochon & D. Ariely (2012).
license: Original summary written for this knowledge base (free to use); cite the original source

author: D. Kahneman et al.
title: Peak–end rule
statement: Experiences are remembered by peak and end.
rationale: Design endings and peak moments.
audit_check: Are journey endings positive and clear?
license: Original summary written for this knowledge base (free to use); cite the original source

author: B. Murdock
title: Serial position effect
statement: First and last items are remembered best.
rationale: Place key items at start/end of lists.
audit_check: Are key items first or last?
license: Original summary written for this knowledge base (free to use); cite the original source

author: H. von Restorff
title: Isolation (Von Restorff) effect
statement: Distinct items are remembered.
rationale: Make primary actions distinct.
audit_check: Is the primary action visually distinct?
license: Original summary written for this knowledge base (free to use); cite the original source

author: B. Zeigarnik
title: Zeigarnik effect
statement: Incomplete tasks are remembered better.
rationale: Progress and checklists motivate completion.
audit_check: Is incompleteness used honestly?
license: Original summary written for this knowledge base (free to use); cite the original source

author: C. Hull
title: Goal-gradient effect
statement: Effort increases near the goal.
rationale: Show progress.
audit_check: Do flows show progress?
license: Original summary written for this knowledge base (free to use); cite the original source

author: R. Buell & M. Norton
title: Labor illusion
statement: Visible effort increases perceived value.
rationale: Show meaningful work during waits.
audit_check: Do waits show meaningful progress?
license: Original summary written for this knowledge base (free to use); cite the original source

author: R. Zajonc
title: Mere-exposure effect
statement: Familiarity breeds liking.
rationale: Follow conventions; brand consistency builds trust.
audit_check: Are conventions followed?
license: Original summary written for this knowledge base (free to use); cite the original source

author: E. Thorndike
title: Halo effect
statement: One positive trait influences overall judgment.
rationale: Visual polish raises credibility.
audit_check: Are there visible quality flaws?
license: Original summary written for this knowledge base (free to use); cite the original source

author: M. Kurosu & K. Kashimura
title: Aesthetic–usability effect
statement: Attractive designs are perceived as more usable.
rationale: Polish can mask problems in testing.
audit_check: Are performance metrics measured, not just opinions?
license: Original summary written for this knowledge base (free to use); cite the original source

source_org: V. Morwitz, E. Greenleaf & E. Johnson
author: V. Morwitz, E. Greenleaf & E. Johnson
title: Price partitioning / drip pricing
statement: Splitting a price into base price and surcharges lowers perceived total cost.
rationale: Hidden fees revealed late (drip pricing) are deceptive and regulated (e.g., FTC junk fees rule 2024).
audit_check: Is the total price, including mandatory fees, shown upfront?
citation: V. Morwitz, E. Greenleaf & E. Johnson (1998).
license: Original summary written for this knowledge base (free to use); cite the original source

author: D. Prelec & G. Loewenstein
title: Pain of paying / payment decoupling
statement: Paying causes psychological pain, reduced when payment is decoupled from consumption (credit, stored cards, subscriptions).
rationale: One-click purchase and auto-renewal reduce friction; ensure transparency and easy cancellation.
audit_check: Are recurring charges clearly disclosed and easy to cancel?
license: Original summary written for this knowledge base (free to use); cite the original source

author: R. Thaler
title: Mental accounting
statement: People treat money differently depending on its source or intended use.
rationale: Credits, points and in-app currencies obscure real cost; show real-money equivalents.
audit_check: Are virtual currencies accompanied by real-money prices?
license: Original summary written for this knowledge base (free to use); cite the original source

source_org: K. Shampanier, N. Mazar & D. Ariely
author: K. Shampanier, N. Mazar & D. Ariely
title: Zero price effect
statement: "Free" is perceived as disproportionately valuable compared to a low price.
rationale: Free tiers and free shipping thresholds strongly influence behavior; "free" must not hide costs or data trade-offs.
audit_check: Do "free" offers disclose conditions (auto-renewal, data use)?
citation: K. Shampanier, N. Mazar & D. Ariely (2007).
license: Original summary written for this knowledge base (free to use); cite the original source

author: I. Simonson
title: Compromise effect
statement: People tend to choose middle options.
rationale: Middle tiers in pricing are often chosen; place the best-fit option for most users there honestly.
audit_check: Is the middle/recommended tier genuinely the best fit for most users?
license: Original summary written for this knowledge base (free to use); cite the original source

source_org: R. Cialdini, C. Kallgren & R. Reno
author: R. Cialdini, C. Kallgren & R. Reno
title: Social norms effect
statement: Descriptive norms ("most people do X") influence behavior.
rationale: Norm messages can encourage beneficial behaviors (e.g., saving, security).
audit_check: Are norm messages truthful?
citation: R. Cialdini, C. Kallgren & R. Reno (1991).
license: Original summary written for this knowledge base (free to use); cite the original source

source_org: S. Bikhchandani, D. Hirshleifer & I. Welch
author: S. Bikhchandani, D. Hirshleifer & I. Welch
title: Herd behavior / information cascades
statement: People follow earlier choices of others, ignoring their own information.
rationale: Bestseller labels and trending lists create cascades.
audit_check: Are popularity labels based on real data?
citation: S. Bikhchandani, D. Hirshleifer & I. Welch (1992).
license: Original summary written for this knowledge base (free to use); cite the original source

author: J. Brehm
title: Psychological reactance
statement: When freedom is threatened, people resist and do the opposite.
rationale: Heavy-handed prompts, forced actions and nagging cause backlash; give choice.
audit_check: Do prompts respect user choice (dismissible, not repeated after decline)?
license: Original summary written for this knowledge base (free to use); cite the original source

author: M. Mather & M. Johnson
title: Choice-supportive bias
statement: People retroactively ascribe positive attributes to options they chose.
rationale: Post-purchase confirmation reinforces satisfaction.
audit_check: Do confirmation screens reinforce what the user gains?
license: Original summary written for this knowledge base (free to use); cite the original source

author: L. Festinger (cognitive dissonance)
title: Post-purchase rationalization / buyer’s remorse
statement: After a choice, people reduce dissonance by justifying it; or experience remorse.
rationale: Clear confirmations, easy returns and onboarding after purchase reduce remorse.
audit_check: Is post-purchase communication reassuring and are returns easy?
license: Original summary written for this knowledge base (free to use); cite the original source

author: L. Festinger
title: Cognitive dissonance
statement: Discomfort from holding conflicting beliefs or behaviors.
rationale: Interfaces that contradict users’ intentions (e.g., keep promoting after cancellation) create frustration.
audit_check: Does the product respect stated user preferences consistently?
license: Original summary written for this knowledge base (free to use); cite the original source

author: B. Fischhoff
title: Hindsight bias
statement: After an outcome, people believe it was predictable.
rationale: Post-launch analysis can be distorted; record hypotheses before tests.
audit_check: Are experiment hypotheses recorded before results?
license: Original summary written for this knowledge base (free to use); cite the original source

author: A. Wald (WWII aircraft analysis)
title: Survivorship bias
statement: Focusing on successes that survived a selection process while ignoring failures.
rationale: Analytics of retained users ignores those who abandoned; research churned users and drop-offs.
audit_check: Does research include users who abandoned or churned?
license: Original summary written for this knowledge base (free to use); cite the original source

author: R. Rosenthal
title: Observer-expectancy effect
statement: Researchers’ expectations subtly influence participants.
rationale: Moderators must avoid leading questions and cues.
audit_check: Are usability test scripts neutral and non-leading?
license: Original summary written for this knowledge base (free to use); cite the original source

author: A. Edwards
title: Social desirability bias
statement: Respondents answer in ways they think are socially acceptable.
rationale: Self-reported behavior in surveys and interviews is unreliable; observe actual behavior.
audit_check: Are key findings based on observed behavior rather than self-report alone?
license: Original summary written for this knowledge base (free to use); cite the original source

author: L. Cronbach
title: Acquiescence bias
statement: Tendency to agree with statements regardless of content.
rationale: Survey items should be balanced (mixed positive/negative wording, as in SUS).
audit_check: Are survey items balanced to counter yes-saying?
license: Original summary written for this knowledge base (free to use); cite the original source

author: Memory research
title: Recency bias
statement: Recent events weigh more heavily in judgment.
rationale: Post-task questionnaires are dominated by the last task; randomize task order.
audit_check: Is task order randomized in testing?
license: Original summary written for this knowledge base (free to use); cite the original source

author: S. Asch
title: Primacy effect
statement: Early information has outsized influence on impressions.
rationale: First screens and first impressions shape judgments of the whole product.
audit_check: Is the first screen strong and clear?
license: Original summary written for this knowledge base (free to use); cite the original source

author: H. Schuman & S. Presser
title: Question-order and wording effects
statement: The order and wording of survey questions change responses.
rationale: Write neutral questions and randomize where appropriate.
audit_check: Are survey questions neutral and well-ordered?
license: Original summary written for this knowledge base (free to use); cite the original source

author: D. Ellsberg
title: Ambiguity aversion
statement: People prefer known risks over unknown risks.
rationale: Unclear pricing, delivery dates or outcomes reduce conversion; be specific.
audit_check: Are costs, timelines and outcomes stated specifically?
license: Original summary written for this knowledge base (free to use); cite the original source

source_org: J. Baron, R. Gowda & H. Kunreuther
author: J. Baron, R. Gowda & H. Kunreuther
title: Zero-risk bias
statement: Preference for eliminating a small risk entirely over reducing a larger risk.
rationale: Guarantees and free returns remove perceived risk and increase conversion.
audit_check: Are guarantees and return policies visible at decision points?
citation: J. Baron, R. Gowda & H. Kunreuther (1993).
license: Original summary written for this knowledge base (free to use); cite the original source

author: D. Galai & O. Sade
title: Ostrich effect
statement: Avoiding negative information.
rationale: Users avoid checking finances/health dashboards when news may be bad; design supportive framing.
audit_check: Is negative information presented supportively with next steps?
license: Original summary written for this knowledge base (free to use); cite the original source

author: S. DellaVigna & U. Malmendier
title: Present bias in subscriptions (trial traps)
statement: People overestimate future usage and forget to cancel ("paying not to go to the gym").
rationale: Auto-renewing trials exploit this; send reminders and make cancellation easy.
audit_check: Are trial end reminders sent and cancellation easy?
license: Original summary written for this knowledge base (free to use); cite the original source

source_org: P. Johansson, L. Hall et al.
author: P. Johansson, L. Hall et al.
title: Choice blindness
statement: People often fail to notice when the outcome differs from their choice and justify it anyway.
rationale: Always show a clear summary of chosen options before commitment.
audit_check: Is there a clear summary of selections before checkout/submit?
citation: P. Johansson, L. Hall et al. (2005).
license: Original summary written for this knowledge base (free to use); cite the original source

source_org: S. Barnes; P. Norberg et al.
author: S. Barnes; P. Norberg et al.
title: Privacy paradox
statement: People state strong privacy concerns but disclose personal data readily.
rationale: Do not interpret disclosure as consent to misuse; design privacy-protective defaults.
audit_check: Are privacy-protective settings default?
citation: S. Barnes; P. Norberg et al. (2006/2007).
license: Original summary written for this knowledge base (free to use); cite the original source

author: E. Langer
title: Illusion of control
statement: People overestimate their control over outcomes.
rationale: Placebo controls (buttons that do nothing) are deceptive; real controls must work.
audit_check: Do all controls (e.g., close buttons, settings) actually do what they claim?
license: Original summary written for this knowledge base (free to use); cite the original source

author: K. Mosier & L. Skitka
title: Automation bias
statement: Over-reliance on automated suggestions.

audit_check: Do AI outputs show uncertainty and evidence?
license: Original summary written for this knowledge base (free to use); cite the original source

author: J. Weizenbaum
title: Anthropomorphism / ELIZA effect
statement: People attribute human understanding and emotion to computer programs that mimic conversation.

audit_check: Does the conversational agent disclose that it is an AI and its limitations?
license: Original summary written for this knowledge base (free to use); cite the original source

author: P. Rozin & E. Royzman
title: Negativity bias
statement: Negative experiences have a greater impact than positive ones.

audit_check: Are severe pain points prioritized over adding delight?
license: Original summary written for this knowledge base (free to use); cite the original source

author: M. McDaniel & G. Einstein
title: Bizarreness effect
statement: Unusual material is remembered better.
rationale: Novel visuals aid memorability but harm learnability of conventional controls.
audit_check: Is novelty used for content/brand rather than for core controls?
license: Original summary written for this knowledge base (free to use); cite the original source

author: Memory research
title: Humor effect
statement: Humorous items are remembered better.
rationale: Playful microcopy can aid memory but is inappropriate in error/serious contexts.
audit_check: Is tone appropriate to context (no jokes in errors involving money, health, loss)?

author: D. Walker & E. Vul
title: Cheerleader effect
statement: Faces appear more attractive in a group than alone.

author: S. Mullainathan & E. Shafir

statement: Scarcity of time or money captures attention and reduces cognitive bandwidth.

source_org: R. Baumeister et al.; S. Danziger et al.
author: R. Baumeister et al.; S. Danziger et al.
title: Decision fatigue / ego depletion
statement: Making many decisions may degrade the quality of later decisions (replication of ego depletion is contested).

author: P. Slovic et al.

author: H. Jenkins & R. Sainsbury

source_org: A. Geier, P. Rozin & G. Doros

source_org: H. Dai, K. Milkman & J. Riis

statement: People are more likely to pursue goals after temporal landmarks (new year, birthdays, Mondays).

source_org: T. Schelling; D. Small & G. Loewenstein
author: T. Schelling; D. Small & G. Loewenstein

title: Pratfall effect
statement: Competent people become more likable after making a small mistake.
rationale: Honest admissions of limits (e.g., an AI saying it may be wrong) can increase trust.

title: Left-digit effect (charm pricing)
statement: Prices ending in .99 are perceived as much lower when the leftmost digit changes.
rationale: Common pricing tactic; not deceptive per se, but contributes to price opacity.

author: M. Janiszewski & D. Uy
title: Precision effect in numbers
statement: Precise numbers are perceived as more credible and act as stronger anchors.
rationale: Specific claims ("saves 37 minutes") are trusted more than round numbers; must be true.
audit_check: Are precise claims backed by data?

title: Noble edge effect
statement: Corporate social responsibility can make products seem better performing.
rationale: Sustainability claims affect perceived quality; greenwashing is deceptive.

title: Belief bias

rationale: Teams may accept weak research that confirms beliefs.

author: Learning/HCI research
title: Novelty effect
statement: Initial performance or engagement improvements fade as novelty wears off.
rationale: A/B tests of new features should run long enough to see past novelty.

author: A. Sedley & H. Müller (Google)
title: Change aversion
statement: Users react negatively to changes initially, regardless of quality, then adapt.
rationale: Expect short-term dips after redesigns; give advance notice, opt-in periods and explanations.
